task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: within-game lineup substitution as causal instrument
methodological_questions: How to isolate the effect of a full five-man offensive change on shot mix from confounding by individual shooter tendencies and defensive matchups?
What is the effective sample size of unique offensive five-man units and transition possessions in three NBA seasons?
How to define and measure shot mix while handling end-of-quarter heaves and garbage time?
What placebo and falsification tests can rule out confounds and mechanical artefacts?
Does the data support a design with sufficient power to reject a null effect after multiplicity adjustments?

historical_evidence.finding: The PULL_UP exposure-effect shrank from -0.0255 to -0.0063 when lineup fixed effects were removed, and a same-shooter placebo on other play types yielded -0.0071/-0.0075, indicating a shooter-level confound rather than a genuine defensive adaptation.

An excess in suppression estimates produced by a selection-on-large-drop rule was reproduced by a within-unit permutation null (observed 0.3798 vs null 0.3744, z 0.40) and removed after centering for drift, revealing a mechanical artefact.

Stacked suppression after opponent POST_UP then PUTBACK was smaller than the additive prediction (-0.071 vs -0.232), but per-player stacked observations often numbered fewer than five, making estimates unreliable.
A penalty-state behavioural contrast (3 to 4 team fouls) was not distinct from adjacent-foul placebos (2->3 and 4->5+), and standard errors were not printed, leaving the effect unclear.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Estimating a play-type-level effect without lineup fixed effects and without a same-shooter placebo
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by shooter selection produced an artefactual decline; the apparent effect vanished when shooter identity was controlled.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Selecting units (lineups) on a large drop and comparing them with matched controls
failed_approaches.why: The selection rule created a mechanical excess that was reproduced by a permutation null, driven by drift and regression to the mean.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing additive stacking of lineup-level suppression effects
failed_approaches.why: Small per-player sample sizes prevented reliable estimation, and one cluster gradient had an unexpected sign, indicating implementation or design sensitivity limits.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Identifying a game-state effect (entering the penalty) without a distinct placebo contrast
failed_approaches.why: The penalty-state contrast was indistinguishable from adjacent changes, suggesting the design lacked the placebo dependence needed to separate signal from noise.

evidence_establishes: Estimates of lineup-level effects on shot outcomes are highly susceptible to confounding by individual shooter identity and must include shooter fixed effects or placebo comparisons ([prior work]).
Selecting lineups based on extreme values (e.g., large changes in shot mix) can produce artefactual results due to drift and regression to the mean ([prior work]).
Stacked or additive claims about lineup changes require per-unit sample sizes much larger than five possessions ([prior work]).
Placebo contrasts using adjacent events or random permutations are essential to validate any detected effect ([prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the offensive five change indeed moves shot mix in the NBA, and if so, the size and direction of the effect.
Whether three seasons of play-by-play data provide enough power to detect the effect after controlling for all relevant confounders.
The optimal measurement of shot mix and the specific categories that would be most sensitive to personnel changes.
own_inferences: The question can be reframed as a within-game causal identification problem: each substitution of one or more offensive players provides a treatment event, and the outcome is the change in shot type distribution relative to the pre-substitution baseline.

With three full NBA seasons, there are many thousands of substitution events, but the effective sample size may be limited for rare shot types and for lineups that appear only briefly; difficulties will arise if the analysis is broken down by specific lineups rather than aggregated across all changes.

The design must incorporate individual offensive player fixed effects (entering/exiting players), defensive matchup quality, game state, and time period, along with placebo tests that randomly permute substitution timings or examine unchanged offensive lineups to rule out confounds.
A demonstration that the shot mix changes after a substitution would indeed validate the design’s sensitivity, provided the falsification tests pass.
uncertainties: Exact number of usable substitutions per season and the sparsity of five-man units for detailed shot mix categories (e.g., play type within shot zone) have not been examined.
Effect sizes (e.g., a 3 percentage point shift in three-point attempts) are unknown; pilot data would be needed to confirm power.
The precise definition of ‘shot mix’ (categories, handling of free throws and heaves) and the baseline period (how many preceding possessions) require specification.
Potential residual confounding from defensive adjustments and game script (e.g., score margin) may bias estimates even with controls.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical retrieval, the study might have been designed without lineage fixed effects and without rigorous placebo checks. The evidence directly shows that omitting shooter controls leads to artefactual suppression, and that selecting on extreme changes or small per-unit counts yields inconclusive or artefactual results. Therefore, the decision now is to proceed only with a design that incorporates shooter FE, a comprehensive placebo suite, and per-method power checks to avoid earlier pitfalls.

blocking_constraints.text: Many five-man offensive units will have few possessions, especially when cross-classified by shot type; rare shot types (e.g., mid-range) may have insufficient counts for within-lineup estimation.

Individual shooter preferences and defensive matchups may drive changes in shot mix, making it difficult to attribute shifts solely to the new lineup composition without extensive fixed effects and defensive controls.
Testing multiple shot types and play-type dimensions inflates the Type I error rate unless multiplicity adjustment is pre-registered.
Although three seasons provide many substitutions, power may be too low to detect small effect sizes after adjusting for covariates and placebo checks.
Game-state drift (e.g., score margin, fatigue, tactical changes) over the course of a game can confound the shot-mix before and after a substitution, even with period fixed effects.

Without a successful placebo test (e.g., no shot-mix change when a defensive substitution only occurs), any positive result could be attributed to general game-time trends rather than a true offensive personnel effect.

prior_work.summary: Previous studies have not tested the specific claim that changing the offensive five moves shot mix. However, they have diagnosed several methodological requirements for such a test: shooter-level fixed effects, placebo tests to rule out confounds, avoidance of selection-on-extremes, and sufficient per-unit sample sizes. These lessons are incorporated into the proposed design.

risks.text: Shooter identity and defensive quality may confound the observed shift in shot mix; omitted variable bias can create artefactual support if not controlled via shooter fixed effects, defensive ratings, and baseline adjustments.

Full five-man offensive lineups change frequently, but some lineups will have few possessions, especially for specific shot zones or play types, leading to imprecise estimates and potential failure of fixed-effects estimation.

If the study evaluates multiple dimensions of shot mix (e.g., restricted area, mid-range, three-point, off-screen, pull-up), false positives may arise unless the testing strategy is pre-registered and adjusted.
Even with three seasons, the small effect sizes typical of personnel changes may require unfeasibly large samples; a minimum detectable effect boundary must be pre-defined.

Game context drifts (e.g., score, time remaining, opponent line-up fatigue) over the possessions surrounding a substitution, which could mimic a personnel effect. Controlling for game clock and score state is necessary.
The credibility of the result relies on a falsification test that shows no change when the offensive five is held constant but the defense changes; failure of this test would invalidate the design.
If the study selects substitutions that followed extreme shot-mix outcomes (e.g., a run of bad shots), regression to the mean could be misinterpreted as a personnel effect.

design.estimand: The average causal effect of a substitution that changes the offensive five (one or more players entering/leaving) on the multinomial distribution of shot types (restricted area, mid-range, above-the-break three, corner three, and play-type breakdowns if powered) for the first five possessions after the substitution, relative to the baseline shot mix of the entering players in the same game-state strata, adjusted for opposing defensive lineup quality.
design.unit: A possession immediately following an offensive substitution, with the new five-man lineup on the floor.
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff games from the 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 seasons. Exclude possessions in garbage time (score margin >20 at any point in the 4th quarter or overtime), end-of-quarter heaves (shot attempts with >47 feet distance and <2 seconds remaining), and substitutions that occur with less than 24 seconds left in a period.
design.power: Pilot simulations using approximate counts from one season suggest that with ~30,000 substitution events, we achieve 80% power to detect a shift of 3 percentage points in three-point attempt proportion at alpha=0.01 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for up to five shot-type categories. For sub-categories (e.g., off-screen threes), power will be lower; pre-registration will specify which categories are tested.
design.controls: Fixed effects: game (or game × period), score margin bin (e.g., -5 to +5, -10 to -5, etc.), offensive player identities (both entering and exiting), defensive lineup quality (average defensive rating of the opponent's current five). Baseline shot mix of the entering players computed from all possessions in the same game-state stratum preceding the substitution (within same game, same score margin bin, and home/away). Also control for shot clock at start of possession.
design.falsification: 1. Placebo test by randomly permuting substitution timings within each game (maintaining the same substitution intervals) and showing no effect on shot mix. 2. Test with defensive-only substitutions (offensive five unchanged) – the null expectation is no change in offensive shot mix. 3. Pre-trend balance check: no significant difference in shot outcomes in the two possessions immediately before the substitution between the entering and exiting lineups after controlling for game state.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a hierarchical testing procedure: first test three broad categories (restricted area, mid-range, three-point) with Benjamini-Hochberg; if any passes, proceed to sub-categories (play types) only for those broad zones with a Holm-Bonferroni step-down, using family-wise error rate of 0.05. Report all p-values and Bayesian posterior probabilities under a weakly informative prior.
design.decision_rule: The study supports the hypothesis if (a) at least one shot-type category shows a statistically significant change after multiplicity adjustment, (b) the Bayesian negative-binomial hurdle model yields a posterior probability >0.95 of a non-zero effect in that category, (c) the placebo tests (permutation and defensive-only) do not reject the null (p>0.1), and (d) the pre-trend balance check passes. If the placebo tests fail or power analysis shows the sample is insufficient for any category, the result is inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 per-game play-by-play and derived possession records as available on 2026-11-02, processed with a consistent pipeline for substitution events, shot classification, and defensive matchup data.
